case_analysis.focal_point: Whether MoneyGram’s unclaimed “official checks” (the Disputed Instruments) are “money orders” (or covered as similar instruments) under the Federal Disposition Act such that escheat priority goes to the state where the instrument was purchased rather than Delaware as the issuer’s state of incorporation.
case_analysis.legal_provision: The Federal Disposition Act (12 U.S.C. § 2501 et seq.) and, in the background, the Supreme Court’s federal common-law escheat priority rules governing intangible property (as developed in Texas v. New Jersey and its progeny) and the Court’s original jurisdiction over controversies between States (U.S. Const. art. III, § 2).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Delaware (as plaintiff in Delaware v. Pennsylvania & Wisconsin and as defendant in Arkansas v. Delaware) argues that the Disputed Instruments should not be treated as “money orders” (or otherwise within the FDA), so the default federal common-law priority rules apply; because the issuer is incorporated in Delaware and the owner/address information is allegedly missing or insufficient for first-priority escheat, Delaware claims the right to escheat the unclaimed amounts (or at least resists shifting escheat to the purchase states).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Pennsylvania/Wisconsin and Arkansas et al. contend that MoneyGram’s Disputed Instruments function as money orders (or materially similar written instruments) covered by the FDA, so unclaimed proceeds must be escheated to the state where each instrument was purchased; they rely on Supreme Court precedent rejecting attempts to bypass the established priority framework and on record evidence that purchaser/sender address information is often collected or retrievable, which reduces any asserted “windfall” to Delaware.

John Roberts.reasoning: Delaware’s strongest point remains the textual one: “official checks” are not expressly listed as “money orders,” so the Federal Disposition Act should be read narrowly and anything else left to Texas v. New Jersey’s common-law rules. But as Justice Gorsuch stresses, the Act also covers “other similar written instruments,” and that language cannot sensibly turn on the issuer’s label where the instrument is prepaid, widely sold, and typically lacks owner-address data—the very problem Congress addressed after Pennsylvania v. New York. Justice Thomas’s original-meaning framing reinforces that “similar” in ordinary commercial usage reaches functionally indistinguishable payment orders, and a nomenclature-driven carveout would recreate the incorporation-state windfall Congress targeted, undermining uniformity and institutional legitimacy. We can keep the holding minimal by deciding only that MoneyGram’s official checks on this record fall within “similar written instruments,” without pronouncing on every modern prepaid product.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Delaware’s strongest textual argument—that “official checks” are not “money orders” and that Congress’s list should be read narrowly—fails to account for the enacted residual clause covering “other similar written instruments,” which at the time would naturally encompass prepaid, transferable payment orders materially indistinguishable from money orders for escheat allocation. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers point reinforces the proper method here: once Congress supplied a statutory rule for this class of instruments, we apply it rather than reverting to Texas v. New Jersey’s judge-made secondary rule that produces an incorporation-State windfall. Pennsylvania v. New York confirms Congress targeted the missing-address problem endemic to these instruments, so allowing a label-driven exclusion would recreate the very evasion Congress acted to prevent. Chief Justice Roberts is also right that a functional reading is administrable and can be kept narrow to the record before us without expanding beyond the statute’s text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Delaware’s best point remains the textual one: “official checks” are not expressly listed, and a narrow reading could route us back to Texas v. New Jersey’s secondary, incorporation-State rule when addresses are missing. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, the Act’s inclusion of “other similar written instruments” is enacted text that naturally covers prepaid, transferable payment orders that function like money orders in commerce—especially given Congress’s targeted response to Pennsylvania v. New York and the missing-address problem. A label-driven carveout would invite evasion and recreate the very incorporation-State windfall Congress sought to eliminate, a practical consequence I find hard to reconcile with a faithful, consequence-aware textualism. I therefore continue to apply the FDA’s purchase-State rule on this record without opining broadly on every modern prepaid product.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Delaware’s strongest argument—textual formalism that “official checks” are not “money orders”—doesn’t defeat the statute’s operative phrase “other similar written instruments,” which invites a functional comparison rather than a label-driven carveout. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively root that functional reading in Pennsylvania v. New York’s historical backdrop: Congress acted to prevent precisely the incorporation-state windfall that reappears when address data is missing for prepaid, widely sold payment instruments. Justice Gorsuch’s point about separation of powers reinforces my view: once Congress supplied an allocation rule for this class, we should not revert to Texas v. New Jersey’s common-law secondary rule simply because a holder rebrands an instrument. Pragmatically, excluding these instruments would shift escheat away from the consumer purchase communities—often including vulnerable populations who rely on such products—and toward a paper-incorporation state, undermining fairness and the Act’s remedial design.

But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the statute’s inclusion of “other similar written instruments” cannot be made to turn on an issuer’s label without inviting evasion and reviving the incorporation-state windfall Congress targeted after Pennsylvania v. New York. Justice Gorsuch’s point also matters for my methodology: once Congress enacted a tailored statutory allocation rule for this functional category, it is less coherent to retreat to Texas v. New Jersey’s federal common-law defaults based on nomenclature alone. On this record, MoneyGram’s official checks are at least “similar written instruments,” so the purchase-state rule applies.

Separation-of-powers principles reinforce that once Congress supplied an allocation rule for this functional class, we should not revive federal common-law priority rules merely because a holder chose a different label. John Roberts.reasoning: The Federal Disposition Act, 12 U.S.C. §§ 2501–2503, was enacted to displace the Texas v. New Jersey federal common-law priority rules for “money orders” and “similar written instruments,” allocating escheat to the State of purchase to avoid windfalls tied to the issuer’s place of incorporation. In Pennsylvania v. New York, 407 U.S. 206 (1972), the Court construed Congress’s intervention in this domain as targeting precisely these prepaid, widely-sold payment instruments whose owner-address information is often absent, and it declined to allow states to recharacterize instruments to evade the settled priority scheme. Given that MoneyGram’s “official checks” function as prepaid instruments used for transmission of money and are materially similar to money orders, a narrow, precedent-bound resolution treating them as covered by the Act best preserves uniformity and institutional legitimacy. Delaware’s attempt to default back to Texas v. New Jersey by labeling the instruments differently would invite renewed interstate conflict the Act was designed to end.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Federal Disposition Act’s text covers “money orders” and “other similar written instruments” (12 U.S.C. §§ 2501–2503), and MoneyGram’s “official checks” function as prepaid, transferable payment orders materially indistinguishable in relevant respects from money orders for purposes of escheat allocation. Reading the statute according to its original public meaning, Congress enacted the FDA to displace the Texas v. New Jersey federal common-law priority rules for this class of instruments and to assign escheat to the State of purchase, preventing the incorporation-State windfall that those common-law rules produced when purchaser/owner addresses are absent. Pennsylvania v. New York confirms that, for these prepaid instruments, the purchase-State rule governs and that States may not evade that allocation by relabeling functionally equivalent instruments. Accordingly, the Disputed Instruments fall within the FDA, and escheat priority lies with the States where the instruments were purchased, not Delaware as the issuer’s incorporation State.

Because Congress has supplied a specific statutory priority rule for this category, separation-of-powers principles counsel applying the FDA as written rather than reverting to (or expanding) federal common law to award Delaware the proceeds.

Reading “money order” in § 2503 to cover only a narrow set of legacy products risks reviving the very windfall-and-uncertainty problem Congress sought to fix in this niche area, and the residual phrase “other similar written instrument” is best read to capture functionally equivalent, prepaid, transferable payment orders sold through agents even if not labeled a classic money order. Pennsylvania v. New York (1972) establishes that federal priority rules exist to provide administrable, uniform escheat rules and rejects efforts to manipulate outcomes based on missing address information; Congress then displaced those rules for this category of instruments by statute, so Delaware’s reliance on federal common law yields when the Act applies. Given the separation-of-powers concerns with expanding federal common law where Congress has legislated, the better reading is that the FDA governs and assigns escheat to the purchase state.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Federal Disposition Act, 12 U.S.C. § 2501 et seq., was enacted against the backdrop of this Court’s federal common-law priority rules and reflects Congress’s judgment that “money orders” and “similar written instruments” should escheat to the State of purchase rather than defaulting to the issuer’s State of incorporation. Treating MoneyGram’s agent-sold payment instruments as FDA-covered instruments best accords with the statute’s text and function and avoids recreating the very windfall-and-administrability problems this Court addressed in Pennsylvania v. New York, 407 U.S. 206 (1972), where the Court rejected attempts to reallocate escheat based on missing address data. The FDA provides a clear, workable rule tied to the place of purchase and commercial activity, consistent with the Court’s longstanding emphasis on ease of administration and equitable distribution in the escheat context. Given that Congress displaced the common-law scheme for this category of instruments, Delaware’s fallback to the incorporation-based secondary rule is unavailable where the FDA applies.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Federal Disposition Act directs that “money orders” and “similar written instruments” escheat to “the State in which such money order, traveler’s check, or other similar written instrument was purchased.” 12 U.S.C. § 2503. Reading that text according to its ordinary public meaning, the Disputed Instruments—prepaid, agent-sold, payment orders purchased at retail and payable to a designated payee—fit comfortably within “money orders” or, at minimum, “similar written instruments,” so the FDA’s specific rule displaces the federal common-law priority rules of Texas v. New Jersey. Pennsylvania v. New York confirms that Congress enacted this statutory scheme to avoid windfalls to the issuer’s incorporation State when purchaser/creditor address information is often unavailable and to tie escheat to the place of purchase. Delaware’s effort to revert to incorporation-based priority because of allegedly incomplete address data is inconsistent with that statutory displacement and with this Court’s insistence on clear, administrable escheat rules rather than fact-intensive evasion.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Federal Disposition Act, 12 U.S.C. § 2503, displaces the federal common-law priority rules for “money orders” and “similar written instruments” and assigns escheat to the State where the instrument was purchased. In Pennsylvania v. New York, 407 U.S. 206 (1972), the Court recognized that applying Texas v. New Jersey’s secondary “state of incorporation” rule to instruments sold without reliable address records can produce inequitable windfalls—precisely the problem Congress aimed to cure through the FDA’s purchase-state rule for this class of retail payment instruments. Given the Disputed Instruments’ function as agent-sold, retail payment instruments used to transmit money, they fit at minimum within the FDA’s “similar written instruments” coverage, and Delaware’s attempt to invoke incomplete address data to reach the secondary rule is inconsistent with the FDA’s purpose and the Court’s emphasis on administrable, equitable escheat rules. Procedural fairness and practical consequences favor applying the FDA so escheat follows the locus of the underlying consumer transaction rather than corporate domicile.
